summary: Agent-UCT searches discrete RAG pipeline configurations (five slots: chunking, query, retrieval, post-retrieval, generation, with components drawn from LongRAG, LightRAG and Self-RAG; 384 raw configurations). It uses UCT tree search whose selection score subtracts a decaying penalty for the marginal cost of executing prefixes not yet cached. Caching and deterministic replay come from the authors' WTB/AgentGit substrate. With gpt-5.4-nano on HotpotQA and UltraDomain subsets, the selected configurations beat the three fixed framework presets on a held-out 30% split (significant on UltraDomain, not on HotpotQA against LongRAG), and sampling-based evaluation cuts wall-clock 4.2x versus full-pool evaluation.

claims.claim: Agent-UCT identifies configurations with the highest out-of-sample performance among the evaluated fixed framework presets.
claims.evidence: Tables 3-4 on 150 held-out items per benchmark with paired permutation tests: UltraDomain F1 0.386 vs LongRAG 0.325 (p<0.0001); HotpotQA 0.576 vs LongRAG 0.530 (p=0.27, not significant); joint objective 0.454 vs 0.421 (p=0.05). Single seed, single model. Because the presets lie inside the search space, this shows recombining components helps. It does not show that Agent-UCT is a better search algorithm.

claims.claim: Reuse-aware regularization makes tree search more efficient than heuristic search, black-box optimization and standard UCT.
claims.evidence: Asserted in the abstract and introduction but never tested. No random, grid, Bayesian-optimization or plain-UCT (lambda=0) baseline is run, even though the 384-point space is small enough for exhaustive grid evaluation. Search quality under the cost penalty is explicitly 'not intended to compare' (§Efficiency from Bipartite Prefix Reuse).

claims.claim: Bipartite prefix reuse reduces logical search cost by 73.6%.
claims.evidence: 10,920 to 2,878 logical cost units under the authors' own cost model, versus an upper bound with no caching at all. This measures memoization, which any cached search would get, not the UCT penalty term. No measured wall-clock or token comparison is given for it.

claims.claim: Sampling-based evaluation gives a 4.2x wall-clock speedup over full-pool evaluation.
claims.evidence: Table 5: 157.6h vs 37.9h, 633.1M vs 110.4M tokens, 228,487 vs 29,056 API calls. Strong as a measurement, but it compares two modes of the same system, and the quality impact of sampling is shown only through the selected configuration's out-of-sample score.

patterns.note: A searched workflow configuration beats fixed hand-designed presets on held-out data (clear on UltraDomain, not significant on HotpotQA). There are no competing search baselines and no lambda ablation, with one model and one seed. Search cost is large: 37.9-157.6 h and 110-633M tokens for a 384-point space.
Cost-aware selection term and thorough token, API-call and wall-clock accounting; whether the cost term helps or hurts search quality is untested.

The optimized object is a fixed linear five-stage RAG pipeline; only component choices are searched, not topology. Post-hoc attribution: the generation slot explains 77-83% of reward variance and retrieval 11-15%; chunking, query and post-retrieval are near zero.

methodology.sample: HotpotQA and UltraDomain stratified subsets, 350 search / 150 test items each; 384-configuration space.
methodology.baselines: Fixed LongRAG, LightRAG, Self-RAG presets only; no alternative search algorithms.
methodology.variance: Single seed; paired permutation tests on test items only (no run-to-run variance).
methodology.ablations: Sampling vs full-pool; logical-cost comparison to a no-sharing bound; no lambda or exploration-constant ablation.
methodology.contamination_controls: 70/30 disjoint search/test split; benchmark contamination of the backbone not discussed.

standards.artifacts: No code link found; details deferred to supplementary materials.

biases.detail: Search is compared only with fixed presets contained in the search space, and the 73.6% saving only with a no-caching upper bound; no competing optimizer.

The headline efficiency number is a logical cost under the authors' own model, not measured cost, and it isolates caching rather than the proposed UCT term. Token F1 on long-form UltraDomain answers (acknowledged).
One search run per setting; no seed variation.
Core efficiency comes from memoizing shared pipeline prefixes, a standard technique, framed as a new 'bipartite reuse graph'.

coi.affiliations: University of Hong Kong; Jiangxi Science and Technology Normal University; HKUST; USTC; NYU.
coi.detail: Academic; WTB/AgentGit execution substrate appears to be the authors' own prior system (self-built infrastructure, not a commercial conflict).

verdict_reason: The central algorithmic contribution, cost-regularized UCT beating other search methods, is never tested: no competing optimizer, no lambda=0 ablation, one model, one seed. The remaining findings (recombining RAG components beats fixed presets on one of two benchmarks; caching saves compute) are modest and specific to RAG configuration tuning, not harness or workflow design for coding agents.
applicability: This has little bearing on whether DAG workflows help the team. If the team ever tunes a fixed retrieval or the pipeline by search, two cautions carry over. First, run a cheap attribution pass before building search infrastructure: here one slot (the generator) explained about 80% of the variance and three of five slots barely mattered. Second, budget for it: tens to hundreds of GPU/API hours and 110-633M tokens even for 384 configurations on a nano model. Deterministic replay and prefix caching of pipeline stages are sensible engineering for any static pipeline evaluation, independent of the search algorithm.
